title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
description: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half
body: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal."Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent."It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

schema.headline: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest

title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
description: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash k
body: European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century. It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.

schema.headline: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster

title: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
description: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since havin
body: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop."I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay. "Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral. Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

schema.headline: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour

title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
description: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to sto
body: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders, Musk said in 2019, while it was still in development.In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.In 2025, Tesla sold just 20,237 Cybertrucks, a decline from 38,965 a year earlier, according to figures from Kelley Blue Book. Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 after commercial production of Cybertruck began in 2023.Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something "straight out of Blade Runner, external".But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it "ugly as sin, external".Several recalls - including in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.  And then there's the price."We need to make it at a price that people can afford," Musk told Wall Street analysts that year - which ended up being $61,000 (then £48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

schema.headline: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

title: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
description: More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, acco
body: More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff."I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying:  "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season."And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said."It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters"."When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.PODCAST: Hear more from Jim Messina on AmericastStaying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said."The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said. Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

schema.headline: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Dona
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job."The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests."Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."Figure caption, Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.Figure caption, What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?Miller's hardline views sets up clash with CongressWhile Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans."Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X.  "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.Image source, Getty ImagesOn Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises."Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle

title: Spate of bomb threats poses serious challenge to airline industry
description: All this poses a serious challenge to the airlines, who have little idea who is causing the severe disruption they have faced almost every day this we
body: All this poses a serious challenge to the airlines, who have little idea who is causing the severe disruption they have faced almost every day this week.Although so far all threats have turned out to be hoaxes, airlines have no choice but take each threat seriously."They have a triage system, but follow the same protocols for each until they are absolutely sure there is no threat," says Marco Chan, a former commercial airline pilot and aviation expert at Kingston University."That could involve a mid-air inspection, but definitely a search once the plane has landed."Passengers might not even know there is an issue until they are told to disembark. It can cause disruption, but that is a small price to pay when safety is at stake", he adds.The sight of sniffer dogs and specialist teams on the tarmac searching for explosives on commercial planes may cause alarm.So far, the disruption too has been limited to the few thousand passengers who have been directly involved.Paul Mason, an aviation security expert, says there will be a financial cost to the airline involved, but planes get diverted every day."The number can sometimes run to over a hundred planes daily, for things like technical issues, medical emergencies, even the weather," he adds. "They far outweigh the few which have been diverted due to hoaxes. So airlines are well equipped at dealing with the unexpected."It is also unlikely that customers will be able to get refunds, he explains, because these incidents are not the fault of the airlines.The more worrying aspect over the past few days will be the seeming random nature of the targets and the lack of any credible intelligence regarding who is behind the threats.Aside from emails suggesting that an extremist misogynist group had claimed responsibility for a handful of the incidents - although since denied by its founder - there appear to be few leads.With 20 years of military experience as well, Paul Mason says the incidents bear the hallmarks of hybrid warfare, which involves unconventional methods such as cyber attacks."It does feel co-ordinated," he says. "Russia has said it's got nothing to do with it, but it could be proxies. It's a very easy way to create disruption and chaos, with plausible deniability.""That's the problem. Someone can have an opinion on who is behind it, but if the perpetrators are using sophisticated technology, it will be very hard to trace them."He does say however that if misguided individuals try to copy the threats they could find themselves in serious trouble.The Aviation Security Act 1982 states that "intentionally communicating false, misleading, or deceptive information that endangers - or is likely to endanger - the safety of an aircraft in flight is a serious criminal offence".The maximum sentence is life imprisonment.There is precious little that airports and airlines can do to guard against actually receiving threats, as they can come from a vast range of sources. But the punishment is designed to act as a deterrent.As Paul Mason warns: "Someone might think it's a laugh and very easy to do, but unless they are very sophisticated, they are highly likely to be traced. And find themselves facing prison."

schema.headline: Spate of bomb threats poses serious challenge to airline industry

title: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason
description: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raise
body: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement."By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement."The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court. He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.But if the four-year sentence is upheld, it would rule him out of the next elections, due in 2030.Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty. Human rights group Amnesty International described his conviction as a "travesty of justice"."Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted," said its regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah:President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years in exile.He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.Last week, Amnesty accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

schema.headline: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason

title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD VanceByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterBallot
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD VanceByBernd Debusmann JrWhite House reporterBallots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes. Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentumSeveral prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger. Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressureExit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio."The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party."The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters."It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for futureBoth the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election."The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earnedBoth parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds. Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm."Neither party owns these voters," she said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina HinojosaThe Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend."Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said."After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

schema.headline: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race

title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
description: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in
body: A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely. No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday. As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them. Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public."Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week. Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities"."The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats."What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

schema.headline: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines

title: US midterm results spark fears in Israel over future of two countries' ties
description: As the US midterm election results rolled in, long-held Israeli assumptions about the transatlantic alliance began to shatter."For us in Israel, this
body: As the US midterm election results rolled in, long-held Israeli assumptions about the transatlantic alliance began to shatter."For us in Israel, this will be a generational sea change," wrote one prominent journalist in Israel's biggest-selling newspaper, right-leaning Yedioth Ahronoth. "The [prime minister, Benjamin] Netanyahu government sowed the wind and reaped the tsunami."Israel's opposition leaders have lined up to blame their prime minister, with one saying the US results showed "just how toxic Netanyahu has become" among both Democrats and Republicans.The prime minister himself has so far remained silent."Israel's political establishment understood intellectually that things have been shifting. They have not understood how much and how quickly," one US official with knowledge of the situation told me.Israel's relationship with the US was a campaign issue in races across America.Many Democratic candidates were sharply critical of Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and the costs of the joint US-Israeli war on Iran was a key issue for many voters.The US president himself blamed the Iran War for the Republican rout – a war that Israel's leader is widely seen as having promoted to him.And US Vice-President JD Vance cited the US relationship to Israel as one of four key reasons voters had deserted the party, hammering home the message that the relationship is now seen as a political problem by its key ally."That might be even worse than what happened in the midterms," Israeli political and security analyst Yaakov Katz told me. "Because the Democrats we knew about, now [Vance] is pointing the finger and saying: 'Our voters want us to change our position on Israel' – and Israelis don't fully understand where this is going."The question plaguing Israelis now is what this means for Israel's security and influence.The sense of staunch US military and diplomatic support had remained unshaken in Israel despite growing anger among US voters, President Donald Trump's public insults to Netanyahu, and differences over Israel's actions in Iran and Lebanon.Israel's prime minister continually boasted of his closeness to Trump, describing his "true friendship" and "unwavering support".And just nine months ago, Israelis watched their armed forces wage war on Iran hand in hand with the US military, as the "unprecedented" coordination of the two allies became a daily mantra among military spokespeople and politicians.So Trump's unexpected statement during a Fox News interview this week that he would stop $3.8bn (3.4bn euros; £2.8bn) in US military aid to Israel two years earlier than planned, caused shock here – not so much for the loss of aid as for what the move said about Israel's status as a diplomatic partner.Israel's president said the announcement came as "a bolt from the blue"."Nobody knows anything," was the headline in a report by Yedioth Ahronoth, adding that officials were still struggling to understand whether Trump's remark was serious, two days on.The Israeli prime minister's office responded to the news several days later, saying that the shift from US aid to partnership showed "the strength and sophistication" of the bilateral relationship.US military aid is less than 10% of Israel's annual military budget. But Yaakov Katz, author of several books about Israel's defence and security, said Trump's announcement was the tip of a much larger question around future funding, arms sales and joint military projects with Israel. All of this could be slowed or stalled by a Democrat-controlled Congress, even without the two-thirds majority it would need to overrule Trump."Everything that Israel used to get in a simpler, easier process will now potentially be much more complicated, and Israel has to be prepared that this is a new reality," he told me."Our entire Air Force is American-made military planes, we're dependent on American spare parts and American weapons. The last three years have shown us how dependent we are on American missile-defence systems. [If] those don't show up at the same pace, that's a real difference – that changes your calculation of what you're able to withstand if you go to war."Katz believes the midterms could also translate into tougher demands on Israel over its actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and a requirement not to undermine an agreement with Iran."Something will change in the US-Israeli relationship, but it's a question of scale," said the US official I spoke to, who was not authorized to speak on the record.  "It means shifting to [being] willing to criticise Israel when it's warranted, but the bedrock fundamental relationship will still be there."In an interview on Israeli television, the US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee signalled little shift so far in core American positions, including on Israel's occupation of the West Bank, describing the sanctions imposed by other countries as "irrational" and counterproductive.Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, told another Israeli channel that Trump would be in the White House for the next two years, and that Israel could "feel good" about the US veto in the UN Security Council – something Washington has repeatedly used in the past to block resolutions that target Israel."But we have to pay attention to the voices – not only in the Democratic Party but also the Republican Party – criticising Israel," he said. "It will be harder for us."Questions over its key alliance have come at a particularly sensitive time for Israel, less than two weeks after its own parliamentary elections left neither government nor opposition with a clear majority. Discussions are now taking place with the country's president, who will decide whether Netanyahu or his centrist rival, Gadi Eisenkot, will get the first chance to form a governing coalition."Under my leadership, we will renew and deepen that [US] partnership, strengthen the bipartisan foundations that have long sustained it," Eisenkot said in a social media post.Another member of his opposition bloc, Yair Lapid, said: "What do we do?""We go back to the rule that worked for us for seventy years, and which broke in 2015 when Netanyahu went to speak against [US president] Obama in Congress. Israel doesn't choose sides in America. We work with everyone."Netanyahu's speech to the US Congress in 2015 is seen as a defining moment in Israel's relationship with the US, when the Israeli leader appealed over the head of America's Democratic president to urge Republicans in Congress not to back a nuclear agreement with Iran.Since then, Netanyahu has increasingly anchored the alliance in Trump's Republican party, even as alienation among Democrats has grown.The US official I spoke to said that, before the midterms, Netanyahu could have improved the relationship with Washington by getting rid of his two far-right ministers."I think everyone understands now it's bigger than [that]," he said.How much the new tone in transatlantic relations will play into the task of building a new government in Israel is being closely watched.Some government supporters argue it has increased the need for political stability, and that Netanyahu provides much-needed continuity and a deep knowledge of the US and its leaders. "We cannot afford to be dragged into endless political disputes and election campaigns," said one opinion writer in Israel's largest-circulation daily, the right-wing Israel Hayom.Whoever heads Israel's next government, its American ally may demand more than rhetoric.In the noisy debate around what this will mean for Israel, the silence of its prime minister – once the whisperer of Washington's elite – is perhaps the most telling voice of all.

schema.headline: US midterm results spark fears in Israel over future of two countries' ties

title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
description: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock val
body: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall. The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI."The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today."I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure."The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said. "We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained."Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

schema.headline: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values

title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
description: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon a
body: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families. In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries". The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood. Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock."The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties". Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".

schema.headline: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say

title: Cornell faculty pass no-confidence vote over leadership's handling of Jane Doe allegations
description: Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault"
body: Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault" after a former student alleged she was gang raped while attending.The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former university and the fraternity over an alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.All seven of the accused have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.Friday's no-confidence vote passed by 75 votes to 50. It is largely symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the power to remove leaders. The resolution states that the faculty senate, which represents academic staff, "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University".It did not make any specific recommendations or suggest what administrators did wrong in response to the accusation.It is a rebuke of university leaders including President Michael Kotlikoff, whom Doe has accused of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.The Ivy League institution in upstate New York has said her account of Kotlikoff's reaction is "incorrect".Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, responded to the vote's outcome in a statement, saying: "We recently learned that Cornell's Faculty Senate made a finding of no confidence in the Central Administration's ability to address the longstanding crisis of sexual assault at Cornell."We believe that the Faculty Senate did not reach this decision lightly and considered all available information."Giuffra added: "We are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."The board of trustees, which does have the power to fire Kotlikoff, said in a statement that it "remains confident" that he and his administration "are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus". Trustees board chairwoman Anne Meinig Smalling, added: "This confidence is rooted not only in the administration's actions to date and plans moving forward, but also in its track record of navigating complex problems."She also said that the vote of no confidence "reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable".Backlash against Cornell has been intense since Doe filed her lawsuit in September. She reported the alleged assault to campus police after it happened but the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time.Cornell, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, has acknowledged it fell short in its handling of her case and has hired a former attorney general to conduct an independent review of the case. It also recently announced a series of measures due assault, including cancelling fraternity parties.New York state prosecutors, led by Attorney General Letitia James, are carrying out their own investigation to decide if criminal charges are warranted. Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that state police would investigate any future sexual offence complaints at the university.

schema.headline: Cornell faculty pass no-confidence vote over leadership's handling of Jane Doe allegations

title: Paul Mackenzie: Kenya doomsday cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison for Shakahola deaths
description: A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them child
body: A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity."The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added. The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration."Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987. Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest". Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court. Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death. One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities. "We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023. Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings."It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence. Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

schema.headline: Paul Mackenzie: Kenya doomsday cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison for Shakahola deaths
